title: Advanced Volume Management & Sharing 🔄
description: Backup, restore, migrate volumes, and share data between multiple containers.

slides.title: Sharing Data Between Containers 🤝
slides.content:
# Multi‑Container Volumes

Start a container that creates data:
```bash
docker run -d --name writer -v shared-data:/data alpine sleep 3600
```

Start another container using the same volume:
```bash
docker run --rm -v shared-data:/data alpine cat /data/file.txt
```

Both containers see the same content. This is how you share state across services.

> Use cases: shared uploads directory, static assets between Nginx and backend.

slides.title: Volumes‑from (Legacy) 🕰️
slides.content:
# `--volumes-from`

You can inherit all volumes from another container:
```bash
docker run --rm --volumes-from writer alpine ls /data
```

This is useful for sidecar patterns (log shippers, backups) but is less common with modern Docker Compose.

> The source container does not need to be running (just existing).

quizData.question: What does `--volumes-from source_container` do?

options.text: Copies all volumes to the new container
Mounts the same volumes as the source container
Creates a snapshot of the volumes

quizData.explanation: It mounts exactly the same volumes into the new container, sharing data.

slides.title: Backing Up Volumes 💾
slides.content:
# Create a Tarball of Volume Data

Since volumes are directories on the host, you can back them up using a temporary container:

```bash
docker run --rm -v mydata:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine \
    tar czf /backup/mydata-backup.tar.gz -C /data .
```

This mounts the volume and the current directory, then creates a compressed archive of the volume’s content on the host.

To restore:
```bash
docker run --rm -v mydata:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine \
    tar xzf /backup/mydata-backup.tar.gz -C /data
```

slides.title: Backup & Restore Demo 🔄
slides.content: Backup a volume and restore it to a new volume:
slides.codeSnippet:
# Create volume with data
docker run --rm -v original:/data alpine sh -c 'echo important > /data/file.txt'

# Backup
docker run --rm -v original:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar czf /backup/backup.tar.gz -C /data .

# Create new volume and restore
docker volume create restored
docker run --rm -v restored:/data -v $(pwd):/backup alpine tar xzf /backup/backup.tar.gz -C /data

# Verify
docker run --rm -v restored:/data alpine cat /data/file.txt

slides.title: Volume Drivers & Remote Storage 🌐
slides.content:
# Plugins for Cloud Storage

Docker supports third‑party volume drivers (plugins) to store volumes on remote systems:

- **Azure File Storage**, **AWS EBS/EFS**, **NFS**, **CIFS**
- **Rexray**, **Flocker** (legacy), **Portworx**

Example with a driver:
```bash
docker volume create --driver rexray/ebs --opt size=20 my-ebs-volume
```

This abstracts storage location; containers see it as a regular volume.

> Use `docker plugin ls` to see available plugins.

quizData.question: How can you store a Docker volume on an NFS share?

options.text: Use a bind mount with an NFS path
Use a volume driver plugin that supports NFS

quizData.explanation: To use networked storage as a Docker volume, you need a volume driver plugin that integrates with that storage system.

slides.title: Cleaning Up Volumes 🧹
slides.content:
# Remove Unused Volumes

```bash
docker volume prune
```

This removes all volumes not used by any container.

Be careful: volumes are not deleted when a container is removed unless you use `-v` flag:
```bash
docker rm -v my-container
```

> `docker system prune` does not remove volumes by default; add `--volumes` to include them.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Name Your Volumes
Always use named volumes (`docker volume create db-data`) rather than anonymous volumes. They are easier to manage, back up, and document.
